7.name: Autonomic and somatic organization
7.can: Contrast the somatic motor system with the autonomic two neuron pathway by neuron count and by effector tissue.

7.name: Sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions
7.can: Compare the two autonomic divisions by CNS origin and ganglion location and predict the effect of each on heart rate and on the gastrointestinal tract.

7.name: Autonomic neurotransmitters and receptors
7.can: Match nicotinic, muscarinic, alpha, and beta receptors to their neurotransmitter, their location, and the response each produces.

7.name: Dual innervation and tonic control
7.can: Explain dual innervation and autonomic tone and predict the effect of removing one division from a dually innervated organ.

7.name: Autonomic pharmacology
7.can: Predict the effect of a beta blocker or a muscarinic antagonist on a named organ from the receptor it targets.

7.name: Autonomic function testing
7.can: Measure heart rate variability and the response to a cold pressor or orthostatic challenge and interpret the result as sympathetic or parasympathetic dominance.

7.name: Hormone classes
7.can: Classify hormones as peptide, steroid, or amine and compare the three by synthesis, storage, and receptor location.

7.name: Hormone transport and half life
7.can: Explain how protein binding in plasma affects the free hormone fraction and the half life and predict which hormone class circulates bound.

7.name: Hormone receptors and target response
7.can: Explain why one hormone can produce different responses in different tissues and relate receptor number to target cell sensitivity.

7.name: Hormone interactions
7.can: Define synergism, permissiveness, and antagonism and identify each in a described hormone pair.

7.name: Control of hormone release
7.can: Classify a hormone stimulus as humoral, neural, or hormonal and trace an example of each.

7.name: Hypothalamic pituitary axes
7.can: Trace a three tier axis from hypothalamic releasing hormone through the anterior pituitary trophic hormone to the peripheral gland and place the long and short loop negative feedback.

7.name: Primary and secondary endocrine disorders
7.can: Use hormone levels at two tiers of an axis to classify a disorder as primary or secondary and as hypersecretion or hyposecretion.

7.name: Posterior pituitary hormones
7.can: Explain why the posterior pituitary is neural tissue and state the stimulus and target action of antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin.

7.name: Hormone assay
7.can: Run or simulate an immunoassay for a hormone and use the standard curve to determine an unknown concentration.

7.name: Hypothalamic pituitary gonadal axis
7.can: Trace the gonadotropin releasing hormone axis to the gonads and place the feedback loops for both sexes.

7.name: Male reproductive physiology
7.can: Explain the control of spermatogenesis by follicle stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, and testosterone and state the roles of the Sertoli and Leydig cells.

7.name: Ovarian cycle
7.can: Order the follicular, ovulatory, and luteal phases and explain how the luteinizing hormone surge is triggered by positive feedback.

7.name: Uterine cycle
7.can: Correlate the menstrual, proliferative, and secretory phases of the uterine cycle with the estrogen and progesterone levels that drive them.

7.name: Pregnancy and placental hormones
7.can: Explain how human chorionic gonadotropin rescues the corpus luteum and state the roles of placental estrogen, progesterone, and relaxin.

7.name: Parturition and lactation
7.can: Explain labor as a positive feedback loop driven by oxytocin and compare the hormonal control of milk production with milk ejection.

7.name: Hormone cycle graph interpretation
7.can: Read a graph of gonadotropin and ovarian hormone levels across a cycle and identify the day of ovulation and the event driving each peak.

9.name: Smooth muscle contraction mechanism
9.can: Trace smooth muscle contraction through calcium entry and release to calmodulin and myosin light chain kinase and explain why the mechanism is slower and more economical than in skeletal muscle.

9.name: Smooth muscle types and regulation
9.can: Compare single unit and multi unit smooth muscle and list the stimuli that alter smooth muscle tone including stretch and local chemical signals.

9.name: Cardiac muscle properties
9.can: Explain how intercalated discs and gap junctions allow the myocardium to act as a functional syncytium and state why cardiac muscle cannot be tetanized.

9.name: Comparison of the three muscle types
9.can: Build a comparison of skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle by calcium source, regulatory protein, control, and speed of contraction.

9.name: Adrenal medulla
9.can: Explain why the adrenal medulla is a modified sympathetic ganglion and compare the duration of its circulating catecholamine effect with direct sympathetic innervation.

9.name: Pacemaker potential
9.can: Explain the unstable pacemaker potential of the sinoatrial node by the funny current, calcium entry, and potassium exit and state what sets intrinsic heart rate.

9.name: Contractile cell action potential
9.can: Diagram the ventricular action potential and identify the ion movement responsible for the rapid upstroke, the plateau, and repolarization.

9.name: Conduction system
9.can: Trace an impulse through the sinoatrial node, internodal pathways, atrioventricular node, bundle of His, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers and explain the purpose of the atrioventricular delay.

9.name: Cardiac refractory period
9.can: Explain why the long refractory period of cardiac muscle prevents tetanus and why that matters for pump function.

9.name: ECG waves and intervals
9.can: Label the P wave, QRS complex, T wave, PR interval, and QT interval and state the electrical event each represents.

9.name: ECG interpretation
9.can: Calculate heart rate from an ECG strip and identify sinus rhythm, tachycardia, bradycardia, and a first degree or complete heart block.

9.name: ECG recording
9.can: Record a lead II ECG, measure the intervals, and correlate each wave with the mechanical event that follows it.

9.name: Cardiac cycle
9.can: Order the phases of the cardiac cycle and state the pressure relationship that opens and closes the atrioventricular and semilunar valves in each phase.

9.name: Pressure volume loop
9.can: Label the four phases of a ventricular pressure volume loop and predict how the loop changes with increased preload, increased afterload, or increased contractility.

9.name: Heart sounds
9.can: Explain the origin of the first and second heart sounds and relate a murmur to valve stenosis or regurgitation by its timing.

9.name: Stroke volume and ejection fraction
9.can: Calculate stroke volume and ejection fraction from end diastolic and end systolic volumes and interpret a reduced ejection fraction.

9.name: Cardiac output
9.can: Calculate cardiac output and cardiac reserve and predict the effect of a change in heart rate or stroke volume on each.

9.name: Frank Starling relationship
9.can: State the Frank Starling law and explain how venous return and end diastolic volume determine the force of the next contraction.

9.name: Preload afterload and contractility
9.can: Distinguish preload, afterload, and contractility and predict how a change in each alters stroke volume.

9.name: Autonomic regulation of the heart
9.can: Explain how sympathetic and parasympathetic input alter heart rate and contractility at the receptor and second messenger level.

9.name: Heart sound and pulse correlation
9.can: Auscultate the heart sounds, locate the valve areas, and correlate the sounds with the pulse and with the cardiac cycle phases.

10.name: Adrenal cortex
10.can: Match the three cortical zones to aldosterone, cortisol, and the adrenal androgens and state the primary action of each.

10.name: Pressure flow and resistance
10.can: Apply the relationship among flow, pressure gradient, and resistance and predict the effect of a change in vessel radius, blood viscosity, or vessel length on flow.

10.name: Vessel structure and function
10.can: Match arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, and veins to their role in pressure buffering, resistance, exchange, and capacitance.

10.name: Arterial blood pressure
10.can: Define systolic, diastolic, pulse, and mean arterial pressure, calculate mean arterial pressure, and explain how it is determined by cardiac output and total peripheral resistance.

10.name: Local control of blood flow
10.can: Explain myogenic, metabolic, and endothelial control of arteriolar tone and predict the local flow response to increased tissue metabolism.

10.name: Capillary exchange and Starling forces
10.can: Identify the four Starling forces at a capillary and determine the net direction of fluid movement at the arterial and venous ends.

10.name: Edema
10.can: Explain how increased capillary hydrostatic pressure, reduced plasma protein, increased permeability, or lymphatic blockage each produce edema and match a clinical scenario to its mechanism.

10.name: Venous return
10.can: Explain the skeletal muscle pump, the respiratory pump, and venoconstriction and predict the effect of prolonged standing on venous return and stroke volume.

10.name: Blood pressure measurement
10.can: Measure blood pressure by auscultation, explain the origin of the Korotkoff sounds, and record the response to a postural or exercise challenge.

10.name: Baroreceptor reflex
10.can: Trace the baroreceptor reflex from the carotid sinus and aortic arch through the medulla to the heart and vessels and state the response to a fall in blood pressure.

10.name: Hormonal control of blood pressure
10.can: Describe the roles of angiotensin II, aldosterone, antidiuretic hormone, and atrial natriuretic peptide in long term blood pressure control.

10.name: Cardiovascular response to exercise
10.can: Predict the change in heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output, total peripheral resistance, and regional blood flow distribution during moderate exercise.

10.name: Compensation in hemorrhage and shock
10.can: Sequence the compensatory responses to blood loss and explain the point at which compensation fails.

11.name: Plasma and blood functions
11.can: State the three functional categories of blood, transport, regulation, and protection, and name the major plasma proteins and the function of each.

11.name: Hematocrit and formed elements
11.can: Define hematocrit and interpret a value as normal or abnormal in the context of anemia and dehydration.

11.name: Erythrocyte structure and hemoglobin
11.can: Relate the biconcave shape and absent nucleus of the erythrocyte to its function and describe how the four heme groups of hemoglobin carry oxygen.

11.name: Erythropoiesis and its regulation
11.can: Trace the erythropoietin negative feedback loop from tissue hypoxia to increased red cell production and state the nutrients required.

11.name: Red cell destruction and bilirubin
11.can: Trace the fate of hemoglobin after red cell breakdown and explain how failure to clear bilirubin produces jaundice.

11.name: Leukocytes
11.can: Match neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils to their defensive function and to the condition that raises each.

11.name: Hemostasis
11.can: Order the three phases of hemostasis, vascular spasm, platelet plug formation, and coagulation, and identify the role of von Willebrand factor and thromboxane.

11.name: Coagulation cascade
11.can: Compare the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways to the common pathway and identify the roles of thrombin, fibrin, calcium, and vitamin K.

11.name: Clot limitation and fibrinolysis
11.can: Explain how anticoagulants and plasmin limit and remove a clot and predict the effect of a drug that blocks vitamin K or platelet aggregation.

11.name: ABO and Rh blood types
11.can: Predict agglutination for any donor and recipient ABO and Rh combination and explain the mechanism of hemolytic disease of the newborn.

11.name: Hematocrit and hemoglobin determination
11.can: Determine hematocrit and hemoglobin from a sample or simulation and evaluate the result against reference ranges.

11.name: Blood typing
11.can: Perform simulated ABO and Rh typing and determine compatible donor types for the result obtained.

11.name: Lymphatic return
11.can: State the volume of fluid the lymphatic system returns each day and trace lymph from an interstitial space to the subclavian vein.

11.name: Innate defenses
11.can: Describe the physical, chemical, and cellular innate defenses and explain what makes them nonspecific and immediate.

11.name: Inflammation and fever
11.can: Order the events of the inflammatory response and explain how the cardinal signs arise and why fever aids defense.

11.name: Adaptive immunity
11.can: Compare humoral and cell mediated immunity by the cell responsible, the target, and the mechanism of elimination.

11.name: Antibody structure and function
11.can: Relate antibody structure to antigen binding and name the mechanisms by which antibodies neutralize or mark a target.

11.name: Immune memory and immunization
11.can: Compare the primary and secondary antibody responses and explain how active and passive immunization produce protection.

11.name: Immune dysfunction
11.can: Classify allergy, autoimmunity, and immunodeficiency by what the immune system is doing wrong in each.

12.name: Growth hormone
12.can: Describe the direct and insulin like growth factor mediated actions of growth hormone and predict the result of excess or deficiency before and after epiphyseal closure.

12.name: Thyroid hormone
12.can: Trace thyroid hormone synthesis, state the metabolic actions of T3 and T4, and match hyperthyroid and hypothyroid signs to the underlying rate of metabolism.

12.name: Cortisol and the stress response
12.can: Describe the metabolic, immune, and cardiovascular actions of cortisol and explain the consequences of chronic elevation.

12.name: Pancreatic islet hormones
12.can: Compare insulin and glucagon by stimulus and by effect on liver glycogen and on plasma glucose and identify the islet cell that secretes each.

12.name: Diabetes mellitus
12.can: Distinguish type 1 from type 2 diabetes by mechanism and explain how untreated hyperglycemia produces polyuria and ketoacidosis.

12.name: Glucose tolerance testing
12.can: Plot a glucose tolerance curve from measured or simulated data and distinguish a normal response from an impaired one.

12.name: Four digestive processes
12.can: Distinguish motility, secretion, digestion, and absorption and identify where in the tract each dominates.

12.name: Motility patterns
12.can: Compare peristalsis, segmentation, and the migrating motor complex by pattern and purpose.

12.name: Neural and hormonal regulation
12.can: Explain short and long reflex control by the enteric nervous system and match gastrin, secretin, cholecystokinin, and glucose dependent insulinotropic peptide to their stimulus and action.

12.name: Phases of digestive control
12.can: Describe the cephalic, gastric, and intestinal phases and state the dominant control mechanism in each.

12.name: Gastric secretion and mucosal protection
12.can: Trace the production of hydrochloric acid by the parietal cell and explain how the mucosal barrier protects the stomach and how ulcers develop when it fails.

12.name: Pancreatic and biliary secretion
12.can: State the components of pancreatic juice and bile and explain how bicarbonate neutralizes chyme and how bile salts emulsify fat.

12.name: Carbohydrate and protein digestion and absorption
12.can: Trace a starch and a protein from mouth to bloodstream naming the enzymes at each step and the transport mechanism at the brush border.

12.name: Lipid digestion and absorption
12.can: Trace a triglyceride through emulsification, lipase action, micelle formation, and chylomicron packaging to the lymphatic route and explain why fat takes a different path than glucose.

12.name: Liver function and enterohepatic circulation
12.can: State the metabolic, storage, and detoxification functions of the liver and trace the enterohepatic circulation of bile salts.

12.name: Large intestine and microbiome
12.can: Describe water and electrolyte absorption in the colon, the contribution of the microbiome, and the defecation reflex.

12.name: Digestive enzyme experiment
12.can: Test the effect of pH, temperature, and substrate on a digestive enzyme and relate the results to the region of the tract where that enzyme works.

12.name: Absorptive state
12.can: Describe the fate of glucose, amino acids, and fats in the absorptive state and identify insulin as the dominant hormone.

12.name: Postabsorptive state
12.can: Explain how glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, and ketogenesis maintain plasma glucose during fasting and name the hormones that drive each.

12.name: Integrated glucose regulation
12.can: Predict the hormonal and metabolic response to a carbohydrate meal and to a prolonged fast and explain how plasma glucose stays within range in both.

12.name: Energy balance and metabolic rate
12.can: Define basal metabolic rate, state the factors that raise and lower it, and explain how indirect calorimetry estimates energy expenditure.

12.name: Thermoregulation
12.can: Trace the negative feedback response to heat and to cold through the hypothalamus and the effectors and explain the mechanism of fever.

12.name: Metabolic rate measurement
12.can: Estimate metabolic rate from measured or simulated oxygen consumption and compare resting values with values after activity.

13.name: Functions and functional zones
13.can: State the functions of the respiratory system and distinguish the conducting zone from the respiratory zone by structure and by role in gas exchange.

13.name: Pressure gradients and airflow
13.can: Apply Boyle's law to inspiration and expiration and relate alveolar pressure to atmospheric pressure at each point in a quiet breath.

13.name: Intrapleural pressure
13.can: Explain why intrapleural pressure is subatmospheric and predict what happens to the lung and chest wall when the pleural seal is broken.

13.name: Compliance and elastic recoil
13.can: Define lung compliance and elastic recoil and predict the effect of fibrosis and of emphysema on each.

13.name: Surfactant and surface tension
13.can: Explain how surfactant lowers surface tension and why its absence causes alveolar collapse in the premature newborn.

13.name: Airway resistance
13.can: Identify the main determinant of airway resistance and predict the effect of bronchoconstriction, mucus, and sympathetic stimulation on airflow.

13.name: Lung volumes and capacities
13.can: Define tidal volume, inspiratory and expiratory reserve volume, residual volume, vital capacity, and total lung capacity and read each from a spirogram.

13.name: Obstructive and restrictive patterns
13.can: Use the ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity to classify a spirometry result as obstructive or restrictive.

13.name: Alveolar ventilation and dead space
13.can: Calculate minute ventilation and alveolar ventilation and explain why slow deep breathing ventilates the alveoli better than rapid shallow breathing.

13.name: Spirometry
13.can: Record a spirogram, calculate the lung volumes and capacities available from it, and compare the results with predicted values.

13.name: Partial pressures
13.can: Apply Dalton's law to calculate the partial pressure of oxygen in inspired and alveolar air and state the normal partial pressures in alveolar air, arterial blood, and venous blood.

13.name: Diffusion at the respiratory membrane
13.can: Apply the determinants of diffusion to the respiratory membrane and predict the effect of edema, fibrosis, and emphysema on gas transfer.

13.name: Ventilation perfusion matching
13.can: Explain how local hypoxic vasoconstriction and bronchiolar responses match ventilation to perfusion and predict the consequence of a mismatch.

13.name: Oxygen transport and the oxyhemoglobin curve
13.can: Explain the sigmoid shape of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve and state the physiological advantage of the steep and the flat portions.

13.name: Curve shifts
13.can: Predict the direction of the oxyhemoglobin curve shift produced by a change in pH, carbon dioxide, temperature, or 2,3 bisphosphoglycerate and state what the shift means for tissue oxygen delivery.

13.name: Carbon dioxide transport
13.can: Name the three forms in which carbon dioxide is carried, state the approximate percentage of each, and trace the chloride shift in a systemic capillary.

13.name: Bohr and Haldane effects
13.can: Distinguish the Bohr effect from the Haldane effect and explain how the two work together at the tissue and at the lung.

13.name: Oxygen content versus partial pressure
13.can: Distinguish oxygen content from oxygen partial pressure and saturation and explain why anemia and carbon monoxide poisoning reduce delivery differently.

13.name: Respiratory centers
13.can: Identify the medullary and pontine respiratory centers and explain how the basic breathing rhythm is generated and modified.

13.name: Chemoreceptor control
13.can: Compare central and peripheral chemoreceptors by stimulus and explain why carbon dioxide is the primary minute to minute drive to breathe.

13.name: Ventilation in exercise and at altitude
13.can: Predict the ventilatory response to exercise and to acute and chronic altitude exposure and explain the acclimatization changes.

13.name: Ventilatory response testing
13.can: Measure the change in breathing rate and depth after hyperventilation, breath holding, and rebreathing and explain each result by the change in carbon dioxide.

13.name: Buffer systems
13.can: Compare the bicarbonate, phosphate, and protein buffer systems by location and speed and explain why bicarbonate is the dominant extracellular buffer.

13.name: Respiratory control of pH
13.can: Explain how a change in ventilation shifts the carbon dioxide and bicarbonate equilibrium and therefore plasma pH.

14.name: Calcium homeostasis
14.can: Trace the response to falling plasma calcium through parathyroid hormone, calcitriol, and the actions on bone, kidney, and intestine, and state the role of calcitonin.

14.name: Kidney functions
14.can: List the homeostatic functions of the kidney including water and electrolyte balance, acid base regulation, waste excretion, blood pressure control, and hormone production.

14.name: Nephron structure and function
14.can: Match each nephron segment to its dominant transport function and distinguish a cortical from a juxtamedullary nephron by capability.

14.name: Three renal processes
14.can: Define filtration, reabsorption, secretion, and excretion and write the equation that relates them for any solute.

14.name: Filtration membrane and selectivity
14.can: Describe the three layers of the filtration membrane and predict which plasma components appear in the filtrate based on size and charge.

14.name: Net filtration pressure and GFR
14.can: Calculate net filtration pressure from glomerular hydrostatic pressure, capsular pressure, and colloid osmotic pressure and predict the effect of each change on glomerular filtration rate.

14.name: Regulation of GFR
14.can: Compare myogenic autoregulation, tubuloglomerular feedback, sympathetic control, and hormonal control and predict the effect of afferent and efferent arteriolar constriction on filtration rate.

14.name: Renal clearance
14.can: Calculate the clearance of a substance and use inulin and creatinine clearance to estimate glomerular filtration rate.

14.name: Clearance and handling inference
14.can: Use a clearance value relative to glomerular filtration rate to determine whether a substance is net reabsorbed or net secreted.

14.name: Proximal tubule reabsorption
14.can: Explain how the sodium gradient drives reabsorption of glucose, amino acids, and water in the proximal tubule and state why reabsorption there is described as isosmotic.

14.name: Transport maximum and renal threshold
14.can: Distinguish transport maximum from renal threshold and explain the appearance of glucose in urine when plasma glucose is elevated.

14.name: Tubular secretion
14.can: State the purpose of tubular secretion and name substances secreted including hydrogen ion, potassium, and organic anions such as drugs.

14.name: Countercurrent mechanism
14.can: Explain how the countercurrent multiplier of the loop of Henle and the countercurrent exchanger of the vasa recta build and preserve the medullary osmotic gradient.

14.name: Antidiuretic hormone and urine concentration
14.can: Trace the response to dehydration from osmoreceptor firing through antidiuretic hormone release to aquaporin insertion and concentrated urine.

14.name: Renin angiotensin aldosterone system
14.can: Trace the renin angiotensin aldosterone pathway from the stimulus for renin release to the effects of angiotensin II and aldosterone on vessels, tubules, and blood pressure.

14.name: Natriuretic peptides
14.can: Explain how atrial natriuretic peptide opposes the renin angiotensin aldosterone system and state the stimulus for its release.

14.name: Potassium handling
14.can: Explain how aldosterone and plasma potassium regulate potassium secretion in the collecting duct and predict the effect of a potassium wasting diuretic.

14.name: Micturition
14.can: Trace the micturition reflex and explain how the internal and external sphincters allow voluntary control.

14.name: Urinalysis
14.can: Perform a urinalysis measuring specific gravity, pH, glucose, protein, ketones, and blood and relate any abnormal finding to the renal process that failed.

14.name: Renal function calculation
14.can: Calculate glomerular filtration rate, clearance, and filtered load from a data set and interpret the values in a clinical case.

14.name: Volume and osmolarity disturbances
14.can: Classify a disturbance as volume depletion or overload and as hypoosmotic, isosmotic, or hyperosmotic and predict the resulting fluid shift between compartments.

15.name: Renal control of pH
15.can: Describe how the kidney secretes hydrogen ion and reclaims or generates bicarbonate and explain why renal compensation is slower and more complete than respiratory compensation.

15.name: The four acid base disorders
15.can: Classify a disorder as respiratory or metabolic and as acidosis or alkalosis from pH, partial pressure of carbon dioxide, and bicarbonate.

15.name: Compensation
15.can: Determine whether an acid base disorder is uncompensated, partially compensated, or fully compensated and name the system doing the compensating.

15.name: Arterial blood gas interpretation
15.can: Interpret a set of arterial blood gas values and match the result to a plausible clinical cause.

15.name: Multisystem integration case
15.can: Given a clinical scenario, trace the disturbance through at least three organ systems and identify the compensatory responses in the order they occur.

15.name: Exercise as an integrated response
15.can: Build an integrated account of moderate exercise across the muscular, cardiovascular, respiratory, endocrine, and renal systems.

15.name: Drawing based synthesis check
15.can: Draw and annotate a homeostatic pathway from memory and explain each step aloud or in writing without notes.
